name: Machu Picchu
tagline: The lost Inca citadel the Spanish conquest never found, still astonishing after more than a century of global fame.
highlight: Watching the first sunlight hit the citadel's stone terraces from the classic overlook, Huayna Picchu's peak still wrapped in morning mist behind it.
shortDescription: The Inca citadel high above the Urubamba River, one of the only major ancient wonders the Spanish conquest never found, and Peru's single most iconic sight.
metaDescription: A Machu Picchu travel guide: the citadel, Huayna Picchu, the Intihuatana stone, food and how to plan a visit to Peru's most famous ancient site.
nearestAirport: Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport (CUZ), via Cusco or the Sacred Valley
knownFor: The Inca citadel, Huayna Picchu, the classic postcard view

image.alt: The Inca citadel of Machu Picchu high in the Andes

intro: Machu Picchu is Peru's single most famous sight, a 15th-century Inca citadel perched on a ridge high above the Urubamba River, one of the only major ancient wonders the Spanish conquest never located or destroyed.

Rediscovered by the outside world in 1911, its extraordinary setting — surrounded by cloud forest peaks, most dramatically Huayna Picchu rising directly behind the ruins — has made it one of the most recognisable images in world travel.

Most visitors arrive by train from Cusco or the Sacred Valley to the small town of Aguas Calientes below, then take an early bus up to the site itself, timed to catch the classic view before the day's crowds build.

whyVisit.intro: Machu Picchu's case rests on being one of the world's great ancient sites, in a setting that lives up to its reputation.

points.title: It's one of the few great ruins the Spanish never found
points.text: Abandoned and hidden by cloud forest for centuries, escaping the destruction other Inca sites suffered.

points.title: The setting is as dramatic as the photos suggest
points.text: Sheer cloud forest peaks surrounding the citadel on every side, Huayna Picchu the most striking.

points.title: The stonework is extraordinary up close
points.text: Precisely cut blocks fitted together without mortar, a hallmark of the finest Inca construction.

points.title: Huayna Picchu is climbable for those who book ahead
points.text: A separate, limited-entry hike up the peak seen in every classic photo.

points.title: It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience
points.text: No amount of photos fully prepares you for standing there in person.

attractionsIntro: The citadel's essential sights combine extraordinary Inca architecture with the dramatic cloud forest setting around it.

attractions.name: The Machu Picchu citadel

image.alt: The Inca citadel of Machu Picchu

attractions.text: A complete 15th-century Inca city, temples, terraces and residential sectors all remarkably preserved after being hidden by forest for centuries.
attractions.tip: Hire a licensed guide at the entrance — the site's layout and purpose are far richer with context.

attractions.name: Huayna Picchu

image.alt: Huayna Picchu rising behind the Machu Picchu citadel

attractions.text: The dramatic peak seen behind the ruins in every classic photograph, itself home to smaller Inca structures near its summit.
attractions.tip: Book months ahead — entry is separately ticketed and strictly limited each day.

attractions.name: The Intihuatana stone

image.alt: The Intihuatana ritual stone at Machu Picchu

attractions.text: A carved ritual stone believed to have served as an astronomical calendar, one of the few to survive Spanish destruction elsewhere in Peru.
attractions.tip: A guide can explain the stone's likely astronomical alignments, not obvious without context.

attractions.name: The agricultural terraces

image.alt: The Inca agricultural terraces at Machu Picchu

attractions.text: A striking feat of engineering, stepped terraces cut into the mountainside that once grew crops for the citadel's population.
attractions.tip: The terraces also served a drainage function, preventing the site from washing away in heavy rain.

attractions.name: Aguas Calientes

image.alt: The town of Aguas Calientes below Machu Picchu

attractions.text: The small town below the citadel, reachable only by train or a multi-day trek, and the base for most Machu Picchu visits.
attractions.tip: The town's hot springs, its namesake, make a relaxing end to a long day at the ruins.

attractions.name: The classic postcard viewpoint

image.alt: The classic overlook view of Machu Picchu

attractions.text: The famous vantage point near the Guardian's Hut, offering the full citadel-and-mountain view seen in nearly every photograph.
attractions.tip: Arrive with the first entry group for the best light and thinnest crowds at this spot.

attractions.name: Machu Picchu's stone architecture

image.alt: Detailed Inca stonework at Machu Picchu

attractions.text: Worth close inspection, precisely fitted stone walls constructed without mortar, a hallmark of the finest Inca engineering.
attractions.tip: Compare the finer, more precise stonework of religious buildings against the simpler residential walls.

thingsToDoIntro: Machu Picchu rewards an early start, whatever else fills the rest of the day.

thingsToDo.title: Watch sunrise from the classic viewpoint

image.alt: Sunrise over Machu Picchu from the classic viewpoint

thingsToDo.text: An unforgettable start to the day, watching the first light spread across the citadel from the Guardian's Hut viewpoint.
thingsToDo.tip: Catch the first bus up from Aguas Calientes, which departs before dawn.

thingsToDo.title: Hike Huayna Picchu

image.alt: The trail up Huayna Picchu above Machu Picchu

thingsToDo.text: A steep, exposed climb rewarded with a bird's-eye view down over the entire citadel.
thingsToDo.tip: Not for those uncomfortable with heights — sections of the trail are narrow with real drops.

thingsToDo.title: Examine the Intihuatana stone up close

image.file: File:Lascar The Intihuatana stone, damaged by JWT when filming and ad campaign here (4548727214).jpg
image.alt: The Intihuatana stone at Machu Picchu

thingsToDo.text: A quiet, reflective stop, standing beside one of the few ritual stones to survive intact from the Inca era.
thingsToDo.tip: Touching the stone is prohibited — a protective barrier now keeps visitors at a respectful distance.

thingsToDo.title: Walk the agricultural terraces

image.file: File:Peru - Machu Picchu 069 - pan of the terraces (7367145284).jpg
image.alt: Walking the agricultural terraces at Machu Picchu

thingsToDo.text: A rewarding way to see the site from a different angle, descending through the stepped terraces below the main ruins.
thingsToDo.tip: Wear sturdy shoes — the terrace paths are uneven stone.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Aguas Calientes town

image.file: File:Aguas Calientes Streets in Machupicchu pueblo (1) 01.jpg
image.alt: The streets of Aguas Calientes below Machu Picchu

thingsToDo.text: A relaxed way to spend an evening, browsing the small town's shops and restaurants after a long day at the ruins.
thingsToDo.tip: The town's hot springs are a welcome way to soothe tired legs afterward.

thingsToDo.title: Photograph the classic postcard view

image.alt: The classic postcard view of Machu Picchu

thingsToDo.text: An essential stop for every visitor, capturing the full citadel-and-mountain view that made the site globally famous.
thingsToDo.tip: The light and cloud cover change quickly — take your photos early rather than waiting for 'better' conditions.

foodIntro: Food around Machu Picchu centres on Aguas Calientes, with options ranging from simple to surprisingly refined.

foods.name: Ceviche

image.alt: Ceviche, Peru's national dish of citrus-cured raw fish

foods.text: Available even at this altitude, though best enjoyed once back at sea level in Lima.

foods.name: Lomo saltado

image.alt: Lomo saltado, a Peruvian stir-fry of beef, onions and fries

foods.text: A reliable, hearty option after a long day of hiking around the ruins.

foods.name: Pisco sour

image.alt: A pisco sour, Peru's national cocktail

foods.text: A fitting way to celebrate after a memorable day, widely available in Aguas Calientes' restaurants.
foods.whereToTry: Bars and restaurants throughout the town.

foods.name: Causa limeña

image.alt: Causa limeña, a layered Peruvian potato dish

foods.text: A light, refreshing option, well suited to a warmer afternoon in the valley below the ruins.

foods.name: Coca tea
foods.text: Useful at altitude, a mild herbal tea served at hotels and restaurants throughout the area.
foods.whereToTry: Hotels and cafés in Aguas Calientes.

foods.name: Anticuchos
foods.text: A satisfying, smoky option found at restaurants and street stalls in Aguas Calientes.
foods.whereToTry: Restaurants and stalls throughout the town.

accommodation.intro: Aguas Calientes serves as the only practical base right at Machu Picchu, with Cusco or the Sacred Valley as alternatives for a day trip.

areas.name: Aguas Calientes
areas.bestFor: Being right at the base of Machu Picchu
areas.text: The only town within easy reach of the site, essential for an early start or a Huayna Picchu hike.

areas.name: The Sacred Valley or Cusco
areas.bestFor: A more comfortable base for a rushed day trip
areas.text: Requires a longer travel day but offers a wider choice of accommodation.

budget.label: Round-trip train from Cusco or the Sacred Valley

gettingThere.intro: Machu Picchu is reachable only by train or a multi-day trek — no road connects Aguas Calientes to the outside world.

options.mode: Train from Cusco or the Sacred Valley
options.text: The standard way in, run by PeruRail or Inca Rail to Aguas Calientes.
options.detail: Departures from Ollantaytambo in the Sacred Valley are generally shorter and cheaper than from Cusco itself.

options.text: A multi-day trek arriving at the Sun Gate above the citadel, for those who book permits far ahead.
options.detail: A profoundly rewarding, if strenuous, alternative to arriving by train.

options.mode: Bus from Aguas Calientes to the citadel
options.text: The final short leg, a winding 20-minute ride up from the town to the entrance gate.
options.detail: Buses run continuously from early morning, with queues forming well before opening.

gettingAround.intro: Once at the site, Machu Picchu is explored entirely on foot, following marked circuit routes.

options.text: The only way to explore the citadel, following one of several fixed, one-way circuit routes.
options.detail: Routes are assigned at entry and cannot be changed once inside, per current park rules.

options.mode: Bus between Aguas Calientes and the entrance
options.text: The practical way up and down, though a steep hiking trail also exists for the fit and determined.
options.detail: Buy bus tickets in Aguas Calientes ahead of your entry time.

bestTime.headline: May to September for the dry season, though visitor numbers are capped year-round
bestTime.summary: Machu Picchu is visitable year-round, with the dry season offering the most reliable views free of low cloud.

seasons.text: The clearest views and most reliable weather, also the busiest and most tightly booked season.
Fewer crowds with still-decent weather odds.
Lush and green, though cloud cover can obscure the classic view, and the Inca Trail closes each February.

bestTime.avoid: Skipping advance booking — essential year-round, since daily visitor numbers are capped regardless of season.

itinerary.title: One day at Machu Picchu
itinerary.intro: A single, well-paced day built around an early entry and the citadel's essential sights.

days.title: The citadel
days.summary: Sunrise, the citadel and the Intihuatana stone.
days.morning: Early bus up and sunrise at the classic viewpoint.
days.afternoon: A guided walk through the citadel and terraces.
days.evening: Return to Aguas Calientes for the hot springs and dinner.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make a Machu Picchu visit noticeably smoother.
tips: Book entry tickets, trains and any Huayna Picchu permit months ahead, especially for June–August travel.
Catch the first bus up from Aguas Calientes for the best light and thinnest crowds.
Bring your passport — it's required to enter, matching the name on your ticket.
Pack a poncho or light rain layer, even in the dry season, given the cloud forest setting.
Hire a licensed guide at the entrance for far richer context than exploring alone.
Wear sturdy shoes — the site's stone paths and terraces are uneven throughout.

faq.q: How many days do you need at Machu Picchu?
faq.a: One full day covers the citadel itself; an overnight in Aguas Calientes allows a more relaxed, unrushed visit.

faq.q: Do I need to book Machu Picchu tickets in advance?
faq.a: Yes, essential — daily visitor numbers are capped, and popular entry slots sell out well ahead, especially in the June–August dry season.
Yes, for those comfortable with heights and steep trails — it offers a spectacular bird's-eye view, though tickets are separate and limited.

faq.q: Can you visit Machu Picchu without hiking the Inca Trail?
faq.a: Yes — most visitors arrive by train to Aguas Calientes and bus up to the site, no trekking required.

faq.q: What is Machu Picchu known for?
faq.a: Being one of the few major Inca sites the Spanish conquest never found, its dramatic cloud forest setting now one of the world's most iconic views.
Around 2,430 metres, notably lower than Cusco, which makes it a comparatively easier stop for those still adjusting to altitude.
